newsitem.title: USA: Flame shoots from head as Florida man put to death.
newsitem.headline: Flame shoots from head as Florida man put to death.

text.p: A bolt of flame and smoke shot from the head of a convicted killer as he was put to death in Florida's electric chair on Tuesday despite appeals for mercy from Pope John Paul II and others.

A six-inch (15-cm), multi-coloured flame flashed from the right side of Pedro Medina's hooded head during the execution, flickering for several seconds as the stench of burning flesh filled the room, witnesses and prison officials said.

"At the time the switch was thrown a flame leaped from his skullcap," a witness said. "Some of the smoke spilled through the vents into our witness room," he added, struggling to describe the experience. "It was very ... not good at all."

Florida Department of Correction spokeswoman Kerry Slack said the execution was not interrupted. Medina, 39, believed to be the first Cuban immigrant ever put to death in Florida, was pronounced dead at 7:10 a.m. EST at the Florida State Prison in the north Florida town of Starke.
The incident prompted a day of debate over capital punishment, as death penalty opponents expressed outrage and state politicians defended the state's electric chair.

Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles said the incident would not cause him to suspend executions, although he issued an executive order on Tuesday afternoon calling for an independent medical examiner to participate in Medina's autopsy.
The state government has asked for autopsy results by April 1.

"You know, putting people to death is not the most friendly thing that you do," Chiles said. "The doctor tells us now, and he was observing the thing and observed Mr. Medina's body afterward, he thinks that the death was instantaneous, he doesn't think he felt any pain as a result of that."

But Kathryn Stoner-Lasala, pastor of the First Presbyterian Church in Cape May, New Jersey, who knew Medina and whose church sponsored him in 1980 when he was admitted to the United States during the massive Mariel boatlift, called the smoke a reflection of the wrath of God.

"If the people of the State of Florida want to know what God thinks about their obsession with the death penalty, they need look no further than Pedro Medina. This was not God's judgment on Pedro, it was His judgment on the execution," she told Reuters.
Republican State Sen. Charlie Crist of St. Petersburg, who has sponsored measures to toughen penalties given Florida criminals, said he had little compassion for Medina.

"I'm not overly concerned. I think maybe we need to get a new chair. This whole thing could have been avoided had Mr. Medina not murdered a woman in 1982. That's the easiest way to stay out of the chair," he told Reuters.
Slack said a security officer had to open a window to let out the choking smoke. "We do not have any idea at this point what happened to cause the flame," Slack said.

Medina, who spent 14 years on Florida's Death Row, was executed for the 1982 stabbing murder of Dorothy James, an Orlando physical education teacher. The execution was carried out despite claims of mental illness by Medina, pleas for mercy from the victim's daughter and a letter from the pope.
In a brief statement just before dying, Medina said: "I'm still innocent."
Florida's three-legged oaken electric chair, built by prisoners in 1923, jolts condemned prisoners with three cycles of electricity, peaking at 2,000 volts.
The chair has malfunctioned before. On May 4, 1990, flames and smoke rose from the head of Jesse Tafero, who was executed for the murder of two police officers in Broward County.

Tafero breathed and convulsed for four minutes as his executioners turned the current off and on three times. His case prompted a federal appeals court to block Florida executions until the malfunction was addressed.

Prison officials blamed the 1990 problem on a synthetic sponge that padded the headpiece worn during the execution. Officials said a natural sponge was used for Medina although part of it burned away while the current was on.

In January, Archbishop Agostino Cacciavillan, the papal apostolic pro-nuncio, urged Chiles to grant Medina clemency, but Chiles denied the request. James' daughter, Lindi James, also requested repeatedly that Medina not be executed.

By the end of last year, more than 300 people had been executed in the United States since 1976, when the Supreme Court restored it as a punishment. Human rights organisation Amnesty International says the United States is among the top five countries in the world for judicial executions.
